[Editor's note: The answer referred to above is as follows:]
1. The final counts of population from the 1961 census are not yet available for any municipality or province. Preliminary figures for individual municipalities were released last fall as part of the normal procedures of taking the census, in order to obtain the comments of these municipalities regarding the preliminary figure as it related to their particular city, town, village, township, etc. These figures, as stated in the published reports, were not intended to be the complete count, since they do not include some persons temporarily absent from their usual homes at the time of the census.
Thus, comments regarding	the preliminary census counts were invited by the dominion bureau of statistics from the municipal officials of some 4,500 municipalities across Canada. This enabled the bureau to explain to the municipalities the census rules of enumeration and procedures which in some cases vary from the methods used to compile local counts or estimates. It also gave the bureau the opportunity to make investigations in the relatively few cases where there was some disagreement before the census figures become final.
1	would like to express my personal appreciation to the municipal officials across Canada who have co-operated so wholeheartedly in this matter. Final counts of population for Canada and the provinces should be available around the end of this month. Final counts for individual municipalities are expected to be released in the immediately following months.
2	and 3. Since the final counts of population for individual municipalities are not yet available, it is not possible to show the differences between the preliminary and final counts.
4.	There is no evidence to indicate that when the final counts of the 1961 census become available there will be any significant deficiencies. The dominion bureau of statistics continually strives to improve on its census methods and procedures from one census to the next. You can be assured that the planning for the next census will be no exception, and a great deal of study and research will be given to the 1961 census results in preparation for the following censuses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PENSION

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to increase the amount of monthly pension payable thereunder to $65 per month.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Martineau in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in October, 1957 I had the honour of introducing in this house, on behalf of the present government, amendments to the Old Age Security Act which increased the level of benefit to $55 a month, lowered the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years, and increased the length of permissible temporary absence of pensioners from Canada from three to six months.
In May, 1960 the government placed before this house a further amendment to the Old Age Secutiry Act designed to extend and improve provisions for the senior citizens of Canada. Through this legislation, payment of old age security outside the country was made possible for the first time in our history. Persons entitled to old age security payments who leave Canada for a few months to escape the rigours of our winter climate now receive their pensions as they would at home. And

lor thousands of older persons who have left Canada to be with their sons or daughters, or who have taken up residence abroad because of health, or for other personal reasons, old age security benefits are now received on a permanent basis.
Today I am privileged on behalf of the government to introduce our third measure in little more than four years to improve still further the position of those members of the Canadian community who during their lifetime have contributed so much to the economic and social growth of our nation. The resolution now under consideration provides for a substantial increase in the monthly pension payment, from $55 to $65. This represents an increase of over 18 per cent in the basic benefit now being provided for more than 930,000 Canadians.
In providing for this increase in the universal old age pension, I would point out that there are two other important aspects relating to the adequacy of income maintenance provisions for Canada's senior citizens. The first relates to those persons for whom the $65 now being provided under old age security and old age assistance proves to be inadequate. As in the past, the federal government is prepared to share with the provinces half the cost of any additional assistance which is needed over and above the basic pension.
Under the federal unemployment assistance program through which this is achieved, there is no ceiling on the amount which the federal government will share in meeting the individual needs of older persons. It is left to the provinces to determine the upper limit of the additional assistance. For example, if a province were to decide that the upper limit should be $85 or even higher in relation to the special needs of the individual pensioner, we would be prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost involved, that is of the cost over $65. The federal government would then actually be paying over 88 per cent of the $85.
The second aspect of making adequate income provision for our senior citizens relates to the question of contributory old age survivors and disability insurance which, as indicated in the speech from the throne, is to be placed before parliament if the provinces view with favour a suitable amendment to section 94(a) of the British North America Act.
The government's objective in this regard is clear cut. Our aim is to have an integrated program of old age income security which, in addition to the universal flat rate benefit, will provide a graduated benefit for all those who can reasonably afford further provision for their old age and who have not already undertaken it under private pension plans or other contractual agreements.
Old Age Security Act
Mr. Chairman, as you know, this government has, through federal-provincial conferences called by the Minister of Justice, been endeavouring to reach agreement on the question of having our constitution amended in Canada. This has been our hope, but we now feel it is necessary to ask the provinces to agree to an amendment to the B.N.A. Act so that we may proceed with our decisions in this regard.
The constitutional question may be raised. When the Liberal government was considering the introduction of unemployment insurance in 1940 the prime minister of the day wrote to the provinces and consulted with them concerning an amendment to the B.N.A. Act. All provinces agreed, and an amendment was obtained stating beyond doubt that the authority for such a program was within federal jurisdiction. Again, in 1951, the Liberal government sought an amendment as a basis for the introduction of the old age security program, and a mutually satisfactory amendment was worked out.
The program the government proposes to place before this house involves the provision of benefits to widows and to dependant children, and benefits to disabled persons under a social insurance plan. On the basis of advice from law officers of the crown the amendment to section 94A obtained by the previous government would not permit the inclusion of benefits payable under certain circumstances to widows and children, nor to contributors who become disabled before they are old. It would be folly indeed to initiate the greatest undertaking Canada has ever made with respect to social insurance without having consulted with the provinces and without having ensured that the constitutional authority for such a program has been established.
The Liberal pension program says that the individual will have to choose between a pension at age 65 or a larger pension at age 70. In other words the contributory pension commences at age 70, but if you want an actuarially reduced benefit you can get it at any time after 65.
This point should be clearly understood by all and not glossed over. Under the program which this government plans to place before parliament if the provinces agree to the constitutional amendment, the age of commencement of benefit for those who have retired is 65. If anyone wishes to receive the benefit at an earlier age, an actuarially reduced benefit may be received as early as age 62. This is the provision available under the old age and survivors insurance program in the United States. In developing a program for

Old Age Security Act
Canada, this government considers this to be a feature which will meet the wishes of the Canadian people.
Retirement at age 65 is the common employment practice in Canada as in the United States. How could one envisage a contributory retirement plan that does not recognize these facts of life? This has been one of the main weaknesses of the existing old age security program, and one which we propose to correct. But we do not propose to do it by making those in the 65 to 69 age group second class citizens by suggesting that they should get less, as is proposed under the Liberal plan. If Canada is going to have a truly contributory plan, how can such a proposal as that be justified? The "six-buck" mentality, the hedging, is still here in this latest Liberal effort. But after hearing that the government's program commences at age 65 with a reduced benefit being available at age 62, as under the United States program, we will no doubt hear that the Liberal plan has been altered once again.
A few weeks ago under the Liberal plan married couples were to get $130 a month, or $65 a month each, and all this was to happen within one year of the passage of legislation. But when the government program of $130 a month benefit for a married couple became known, the Liberals suddenly decided that their proposal of only a few weeks earlier was not really enough, that the senior citizens of Canada had risen in their estimation and, as a result, married couples would now be offered $140 a month. And in announcing this sudden change of heart the hon. member for Essex East, at last week's Liberal conference, said the Liberals were spurning the cynical competition of seeking votes by making promises to the older people of our country. What could be more cynical than this remark?
We anticipate that in due course the government program will be placed before this house for consideration. At that time the benefit formulae, illustrations of what benefits will be payable for different persons, will be given. I can assure hon. members that the minimum benefit will be over and above the bare $65 a month, so that persons who have been in a relatively low income throughout their working life will receive a reasonable income from this source. At the same time there will be a spread in the amount of benefit which will relate the amount of benefit to previous contributions.
I can assure the committee, too, that the program will not take a long period before contributors will be eligible for benefits. We recognize that adequate benefits must be available not only for persons who are now 70 years of age and over, but also for the many persons who are now in their fifties
[Mr. Monteith (Perth).[
and sixties, and that determining when partial and full benefits must commence is an important consideration. The provision made in the Old Age Security Act will form part of a new and extended program so that those 70 years of age now and those reaching 70 in future years will continue to receive the flat rate universal payments.
In this context the amendment presently before the committee represents a simple, straightforward next step which can be considered now while efforts to bring into being this more complex and broader program are being pressed forward.
As far as the present pension increase is concerned, it will result in a substantial rise in expenditures under the Old Age Security Act. Current outlays under this program in this fiscal year are estimated at $606 million. The increase in expenditures arising from a growth in the number of persons in this age group will raise old age security payment costs to $623.3 million in 1962-63. The additional cost of the $10 a month increase in benefits will be about $113.4 million, bringing total outlays to some $737 million.
Mr. Chairman, the Old Age Security Act was passed about a decade ago. For almost six years after the introduction of this legislation no further legislative action was taken by the previous government to improve it or to provide a more adequate level of benefit than the $40 a month that had been in effect under the previous old age pension program. Then a meagre $6 a month was budgeted for our older people, even though the federal treasury had a substantial budgetary surplus.
With the present amendment, this government seeks the approval of parliament for its third effort in just over four years to improve the lot of pensioners across Canada. These added costs, I would emphasize, are not undertaken lightly. But having regard for the relationship between present day living costs and the income of the great bulk of our senior citizens, we feel sure that the people of Canada will endorse this step.
Together with similar actions we are proposing under the other assistance programs and our plans for contributory social insurance, this amendment represents a further phase in a sequence of legislative developments which we hope, with the co-operation of the provinces, will lead to an integrated and expanded program, a program capable of providing an increasing measure of social justice for all Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, it is my belief that the resolution now before the committee merits the support of all hon. members. I will, of course, have more to say when the bill is

brought down, but I think I have given sufficient explanation at this stage to justify approval in principle of this latest endeavour on behalf of the senior citizens of Canada.

Hon. gentlemen opposite make much of what they have done. I think it is well for us to consider what the balance sheet in this regard really indicates.

Old Age Security Act
When the legislation arising out of this resolution has been approved the Conservative government that has emulated the Liberal government in introducing amendments to Liberal legislation will have increased old age pensions by $19 a month from the amount in 1957 to the proposed amount of $65, so this government's share of the pension will therefore be 30 per cent. But, Mr. Chairman, that is not the whole story, and no one knows this better than the Minister of Finance. Then the Prime Minister was able to get Professor Clark to make the study. There was then no suggestion as to how long Professor Clark would take, although everyone expected that since the Prime Minister had laid down four months as the period in which the study must be made, that was going to be done. Curiously enough, this coincided almost to the day with the time when the election was held. We did not get the report of Professor Clark when we reconvened shortly after the election of 1958. It was a long time before we received an assurance from the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the report was finally in his possession but we were informed he had not completed his study of the report. No one ever will forget how day after day, session after session, after Professor Clark had made his report, the Minister of National Health and Welfare would say that he was studying the report and just as soon as the report had been studied the house would be advised of the government's position in connection therewith.

Mr. Chairman, we have just been given a fair example of why old age pensioners find themselves in the plight in which they are in this country at the present time. When I heard the hon. member for Essex East say that the Liberal share of the old age pension was $46 and the Tory share was $19, I just wondered when consideration was going to be given to when the old age pensioner was going to get his share. If half the thought, time and energy were being directed toward the share belonging to the elder citizens of this country, I think conditions would improve very quickly.
Before I go any farther I should like to welcome this measure. This $10 per month increase is very welcome to the old age pensioner, and is something that has been long overdue. We only have to go back to the session of 1957-58 when the last $9 increase was granted. Most of us who were here at that time clearly recall the words of the Prime Minister that this was only a temporary measure and there was going to be a better adjustment when we had time to look things over. Of course no mention was made of when this was going to be done. They did not

Old Age Security Act
say the old age pensioners would have to wait until another election before the adjustment would be made.
You know, Mr. Chairman, the present government is threatening to steal completely the social security rut that was carved so deeply by the former Liberal government. Let us make a brief resume of the history of this rut. If we go back we find that the old age pension was originally inaugurated to coincide with the federal election of 1926, when the pension was set at $20. Then in conjunction with the general election of 1940 we had the introduction of the Unemployment Insurance Act. There was a $5 increase in the old age pension in 1943, right after the Liberals lost the Ontario election and the government was formed with 38 Conservative members and 34 C.C.F. members in opposition. The Liberals were practically wiped out, so we got an increase in the old age pension.
Then family allowances were introduced to coincide with the general election of 1945. In 1949 another general election year, there was an increase of $10 in the old age pension. We had another $6 increase to coincide with the 1957 election, at which we also got a hospital insurance program, tightly tied with strings. I have not made a minute study, but as the result of a brief check I find that the only measure that was not introduced to coincide with an election under the Liberal regime was the Old Age Assistance Act, which was passed in 1951. Unfortunately the present government are taking care of this oversight because now they are making that part of the political treadmill.
Today, Mr. Chairman, we had an outline from the hon. member for Essex East of what the Liberals are promising this year. If those of us who are old enough would cast our memories back to 1919-when incidentally I was two years old-they would recollect that was when the Liberals promised health insurance. I do not see any reason why we should take this promise any more seriously than we should have taken that one at that time.
As I said, I regret that the present government seems to have fallen so deeply into this rut. What do we see as a result of their relatively short term in office. We had a $9 increase in old age pensions to coincide with the election of 1958, plus a promise of a raise in the future. Of course the strings were removed from the hospital insurance plan at that time, too. Now we get an increase in the old age pension, again to coincide with the election of 1962. As I said, unfortunately old age assistance, blind pensions, disability pensions, apparently all are to be thrown on to the political treadmill. It seems that the best the elderly people of this country can hope for under either a Liberal or a Conservative 
government is that they will be able to live until another election comes along. In fact, if things carry on as they have in the past I would advise them, instead of going for an increase, to go for having an election every year and then their needs would be looked after.
Having congratulated the government on this measure at this time, I think it also deserves some criticism. I say that because this measure, as with other plans in the past, is not really based on anything at all other than an election gimmick. It bears no relation to the needs of our senior citizens; it bears no relation to their present standard of living; it bears no relation to their present salaries. Therefore I feel that what the minister said about this future contributory pension is correct and it will be a much better solution than any plan we have had in the past with regard to our old age pensioners.
As far as our old age pensioners are concerned, I think first of all a proper basis should be set for our elderly citizens, a proper minimum, and this minimum should have some relation to just what is needed and what is necessary so that our senior citizens can live in some dignity in this country. I think that is one thing that has never been done in the past. In addition to this, I heartily concur with the minister in the idea that some kind of a contributory plan should be made available over and above this basic minimum pension. Of course we have advocated this for many years. It is amazing how rapidly, when election time comes along like this and it becomes time for some action to be taken in the social security field by either of the old parties, they turn to the plans proposed by the former C.C.F. party and the now New Democratic party to get ideas for their plans.
As I listened to the hon. member for Essex East I could not help thinking about this document I have here, which is a draft policy statement written some years ago of the C.C.F. national superannuation plan. It is marked "confidential". I am just wondering whether the hon. member had access to this confidential document, though I think the confidential aspect of this document has long passed. However, it is amazing how the plan unfolded by the hon. member was almost word for word as is contained in this document. What really amazed me was that it was this document, or a very slightly amended document, that the Leader of the Opposition as late as last fall called completely irresponsible. I wonder whether the rapidly approaching election tended to change the value of responsibility as far as the Liberal party is concerned.

I should like to mention briefly a few of the things that we feel should be in this contributory plan. For example, we feel that it should be based on total contribution of 10 per cent of an employee's earnings, made up of 4 per cent by the employee and 4 per cent by the employer. Some may say, why should this be? I think it is generally accepted across the country today that employers have some responsibility toward making provision for the pension or retirement benefits of their employees. In addition to this 8 per cent, 2 per cent should be contributed by the federal government, making a total contribution of 10 per cent.
For self-employed people such as farmers, businessmen, etc., the contribution could be on the basis of 6 per cent by individual and 4 per cent by the federal government. This would result in a nation-wide plan which could be handled out of a nation-wide fund. People not earning enough to pay income tax would not be required to pay premiums. I think in our society today the closest assessment we have of what is needed for a person to live in this country is the income tax deduction. I think income tax deductions are based on the very minimum that is required for people to live at any kind of a decent standard in the country today.
Of course with regard to those people who never earned enough to pay income tax or to make contributions to this pension fund, they would qualify for the flat rate old age pension, which we feel, and have felt for some time, should be this figure that has suddenly come to the Liberals. Five years ago we were advocating that at that time it took $75 a month as a minimum for old age pensioners to try and maintain themselves. I am of the opinion, while we have no figures to back it up, that if a survey were made at the present time we would find that even the figure of $75 has slipped behind today's cost of living and is not in keeping with our present gross national product figure.
The question may arise, what about the present pension plans in this country? Goodness knows there are a myriad of them. There are private insurance plans, industrial plans, even union pension plans among the membership of the unions themselves, the M.P.'s pension plan, government annuities, and so on and so forth. Where would these fit in with a plan such as we envisage? We feel that the workers who are now covered by a pension plan should have the choice of remaining in their present plan or coming into this national pension plan, provided the standards of their present plan meet the standards required by the national plan. If they so desired they could join the national
Old Age Security Act
plan, but they must be assured at all times that their equity can be transferred to this plan. This would result in no loss of equity such as we have seen happen so often in the past and which we see happening on such a widespread scale at the present time. With regard to people who leave their employment for any reason at all, in far too many cases we find they have lost any benefits they may have built up while they participated in a particular plan.
This plan would also provide for complete mobility in our labour force. In many cases today we find people who would like to leave the employment they are in and seek some other employment for which they might be better suited. In so many cases we see what are popularly referred to as square pegs in round holes, or vice versa. In so many cases where there is some kind of a pension plan at the present time, these people are prevented from making a transfer which might be in the best interests of both themselves and the country in which they live. They are prevented from doing this by the pension plans which are now in effect in so many places.
I think that, most important of all, it would alleviate to a great extent the present problem of men over 45. I believe this is one of our greatest problems in connection with men of 40 to 45 years of age. Perhaps their industry has closed down; perhaps they have been forced out of work by automation. There are any number of reasons why men of this age may find themselves out of work. If you talk to any employer he will tell you that in most respects he would prefer to have a man of 45 rather than a man of 20 or 21 years of age because the older man is better trained and is more stable. But unfortunately they cannot do it because either they have a pension plan into which the man who is over 45 years of age would not fit, or they are afraid that within the next year or two they may be forced to enter some kind of pension plan where the contributions for an older employee would be too expensive.
This is one of the major reasons for the difficulties which men over 45 years of age experience today. If this government would take the lead in setting up machinery to provide a nation-wide pension plan under which benefits could be carried from job to job, it would certainly relieve, if not remedy, this particular bottleneck.
There is another important point which should be considered and incorporated in any such plan as is envisaged, namely the question of survival benefits. On the death of a husband, the wife or beneficiary should get the total premium benefits accumulated by

Old Age Security Act
the employee. If the widow should die leaving children under the age of 21, any remaining benefits should accrue to them.

That would do away with some of the idiotic clauses we find in some pension plans across this country at the present time. We need go no further than to look at the present pension plan set up for members of this house to find clauses of the kind I have in mind. At the present time when the pensions of hon. members are paid and they are ready for retirement, either voluntarily or by compulsion, if an hon. member should pass away before he drew one pension cheque, his beneficiary would get all the money paid in to the fund by him over the years plus interest. However, should he have drawn one pension cheque his beneficiary would receive nothing. That is one of the anomalies which would be eliminated by the introduction of a sound and equitable pension plan available to all from coast to coast across this country.
There is a further clause which should receive consideration, and that has to do with the death benefit. We propose that this death benefit should be four times the amount of the monthly pension received by the individual up to a maximum of $600. This sum would be for the purpose of defraying any additional costs due to illness or death, and for assisting to pay the funeral costs. This is a matter which is of great importance, and it should receive full consideration before any pension plan is adopted.
There is one other point which we should consider. If we incorporated a plan of the kind now proposed, people paying into the fund across this country would provide the government with tremendous resources for capital development. In this manner the citizens of this country would be benefited in two ways.
Once more I should like to congratulate the government on this move, even though it may be tardy and inadequate. We look forward with great interest to learning the details of the plan which was outlined by the minister with regard to a contributory pension program.

This amendment is one of the most welcome measures to come out of the speech from the throne, and I should like to congratulate the government and the Minister of National Health and Welfare on bringing it in.
Many older people live in my riding of York-Humber. One reason for this is that we have a senior citizens' project there called 
Beech Hall apartments, where accommodation is offered at a price which the older people can afford. A project of this kind is, I believe, one of the finest contributions that government can make toward the happiness of our senior citizens. This particular building was made possible by three levels of government, and it was the first such block of apartments to be financed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There was one man who led the way in the construction of Beech Hall. He was the reeve of York township at that time and today he is the member of parliament for York South, Mr. William Beech. Because of the energy and leadership that he poured into the project, a grateful community called it Beech Hall. Then with the redistribution, because of the way geography goes, Beech Hall ended up in my constituency.
I have a filing cabinet in my House of Commons office filled with letters from the residents of Beech Hall. They are a gallant and uncomplaining lot of people, but most of them have to live on their old age pensions and from time to time I receive pitiful examples of how they must apportion their budgets. That is why I am especially happy that the old age pension is to be raised another $10 to $65 a month.
It is good to hear that this government is to introduce a contributory system so that every Canadian can build up his own pension. Surely it would be much better for a union to build up the security of its members rather than contribute to the insecurity of socialism. I believe that under such a scheme we could build up a pension fund which would give Canadians a generous old age pension in addition to the basic government pension. In due course they would

speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of a matching centennial grant of a sufficient amount for the construction of a coliseum with at least 14,000
Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum
seats in Vancouver to better serve British Columbia as an international trade, convention, tourist and business centre.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of addressing the house on this resolution, which undoubtedly will be of substantial interest in Vancouver and in my home province of British Columbia. My own thoughts in connection with a proposed coliseum building are contained in two editorials which appeared in the Ottawa newspapers, one in the Journal and the other in the Citizen, about a year ago. One editorial said this:
The purpose of special buildings for the centenary is to leave behind a heritage for future generations that the community might not otherwise have. An auditorium and concert hall should be built in Ottawa, so that centenary observances could be held in adequate quarters. Other cities could also use such facilities.
The other editorial said Canada should:
-"plan ahead to get internationally important conventions and meetings held in Canada in 1967.
For an event of such magnitude, farsighted, vigorous planning is essential. Government, business, cultural organizations-all must work in close co-operation and harmony. Canada should bring the world to her door in 1967. We must start to plan NOW."
In that regard I feel that the citizens of Vancouver are anxious to plan now in order to properly celebrate the centennial in 1967. The type of building that I have in mind in part is somewhat like Maple Leaf gardens. Whenever I am in Toronto on Saturday night it is a pleasure to witness the opening ceremonies in that building. It is my hope that some day all young Canadians will have the opportunity of being there during the start of a hockey game, when the house lights are turned down, the military band is there and the flag is flying in the breeze. It is a very emotional sight and I hope that in due course we will have that kind of building in order that we may experience in British Columbia that which a visitor to Toronto can experience.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) will remember that before the arena fire in 1934 we had a coliseum seating some 10,000 persons which served us very well in those early years. Ever since we have been talking about a larger coliseum in which to handle all the national and international events that we plan for our area. No building in western Canada has received so much publicity and so much comment, good, bad or indifferent. No proposed building has given so much cause for despair and so much cause for hope. The building, or lack of it, has been a major civic issue for a generation. It has defeated mayors and elected councils. It has caused a rash of political promises. The building has been an issue at every level of government in British Columbia and most certainly it has attracted the favourable or
548	HOUSE OF
Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum unfavourable attention of many federal government departments here for over a quarter of a century.
Vancouver, Canada's third largest city, needs a large coliseum. We cannot all agree on its exact size, but we all agree that we at least need something larger than we have at the present time. Everyone concedes the fact that we need a place in which to celebrate. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other federal cabinet ministers who have been on the west coast and have spoken in the present building know what it is like. It has often been described as a cold and drafty igloo. In saying this I am not criticizing those who at present operate the Vancouver forum. I think all hon. members from British Columbia will agree that the Pacific National exhibition directors have tried hard with the equipment and buildings at their disposal.
Ministers, past or present, who have visited the west coast will know that it is no building in which to host the major events of the day. They will know that the citizens of western Canada will never be inspired by national or international programs in a building of this kind. Last summer we witnessed the Red Army chorus in the Vancouver forum while the citizens sweltered in the heat of the building. Then later on Harry Belafonte and Miriam Makiba entertained us there to capacity crowds under most adverse conditions. Entertainers who visit us there hope we will have a much better building. They know that the citizens of western Canada will never be inspired by that type of building and the present conditions. This spells out the need for action in city, provincial and federal planning. Vancouver is far removed from other large Canadian coliseums, and there is thus an unhealthy concentration of national events in the populated centres of the east.
Empire stadium in Vancouver, I am sure, has done much for Canada and has contributed greatly to national unity. That stadium and the competition for the Grey cup have done more for the morale of the people of this country than any other single event. When the Grey cup game was played in Vancouver it attracted a larger audience of Canadians than any other single event. It is good once in a while for people in the east to look to the west for an event such as this. Possibly all too often we have occasion to look to the east for these major spectacles.
A new coliseum in Vancouver, a matching piece to the Empire stadium, could make an almost equal contribution. You cannot build a nation by staging all the big events in the east, and we all look forward to seeing national events, whether they be figure skating finals, hockey or lacrosse finals, again in the
[Mr. Taylor.l

west. At the present time we have not the facilities for staging such events.
As I have mentioned, we cannot build a nation by staging all the big events in the east. Vancouver can do for Canada what Los Angeles has done for the United States. We need a coliseum in which to trumpet our glories. We in the west want to see, at least once in a while, our national and international sports stars, entertainers and political leaders come into Vancouver and speak or entertain us under favourable, and not unfavourable conditions. We would like to see our champions in action. The feel of the champion as reflected in the citizen pays off nationally as well as individually.
The tourist trade is very important to us in Vancouver and if we are to keep pace with rugged, if not murderous competition from other cities in the western United States we must have a convention type coliseum. Seattle, Washington, with the hosting of a world's fair there, will give us keen competition in that area. San Francisco has adequate convention facilities, as has Los Angeles, and Portland is now becoming a real competitor in our area.
I should like to point out that in Seattle, a city of almost equal size to Vancouver, the United States federal government has appropriated $9 million for the planners of the Seattle world's fair. I should also like to point out that in the Toronto area-this was mentioned in a press report-625 conventions bring $96.5 million in cash into that city. We in our area would like to feel we can do more to attract other conventions, particularly from the Pacific northwest.
With reference to the tourist industry, the following was mentioned in an address by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) when referring to that industry:
Only wheat and newsprint bring in more money from outside Canada than do visitors. Only newsprint brings in more money from the United States than does the visitor industry .. . Tourism means much to Canada, but it could mean a great deal more if the tourist industry were more adequately equipped to meet competition in the international market.
Then another report, the Ingledow report, has this to say:
It is not unreasonable to assume, making allowances for available hotel accommodation, that Vancouver with a new coliseum would attract in the order of 30,000 additional convention delegates annually which would represent over $3,500,000 in increased value to the city.
We must keep pace with present developments or forfeit our tourist dollar. Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Los Angeles are now equipped with coliseums and there is an urgent need for Vancouver to be assisted

in this respect. Vancouver can no longer be a whistle stop in the travel folder of convention sites.
There is much truth in the verse:
He who whispers down the well About the goods he has to sell,
Will never reap those golden dollars Like he who stands and hollers!
In my opinion, Canada and Vancouver have to stand and holler about the goods they have to sell at this time. There is no question about our need for a coliseum. If we are to reach our manifest destiny, if we are to do the job we should and can do, we need federal help in building our coliseum. Times and events have changed. No longer will just an ordinary arena suffice. If an ordinary arena could serve, then I am sure it could be built by private enterprise. But we need facilities far better than those which private enterprise could now afford. I do not think it would be any longer possible for private enterprise to construct a building such as Maple Leaf gardens in the west today. The tax situation has changed; building costs have gone up and it is now necessary that we call upon the senior levels of government to assist us. The citizens in our area have shown great civic pride but they cannot raise sufficient funds from taxes to build the type of building which is needed. The project will cost some $9 million. The city is prepared to grant the necessary land and amenities to a value of $1.8 million. Should the federal government make a grant-and I suggest it should be $3.5 million-I am confident that local business, insurance companies and private industry, with or without help from the provincial government, could do the rest. In other words, if the senior government would resolve to assist by making a grant of $3.5 million the project could get under way by April, 1963. The project turns on the help that can be given by this house.
Investing federal dollars in a Vancouver coliseum is wise economics. Vancouver is a port city and we could make a good case based on our geographical position as well as on account of our climate and the natural attributes of the city. Vancouver is important as a trading centre and could well claim and support an international Pacific trade fair, which might not be a bad idea when we are considering the centennial celebrations in 1967. From the results of such a trade fair, if we had the necessary coliseum, all Canada would benefit. It was said in a recent address given by the president of the Pacific and Orient Lines:
Vancouver is one of the major gateway ports of North America's west coast. It will serve a major role in this growth of Pacific travel.
549
Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum
It is a role, moreover, that will bring many benefits, but it also will bring many problems.
Then the speaker referred to the steamship lines and said:
Of the steamship lines, it is interesting to note that Pacific and Orient Lines brought about 10,000 people to Vancouver in 1959, and that some 6,000 people used Vancouver as an embarkation point.
We could use an influx of people as large as this in connection with the type of trade fair to which I have just referred.
In asking for a grant of $3.5 million, citizens of Vancouver are not unmindful of contributions which have been made by the federal government in other parts of the country. I refer, for example, to an article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun dated January 27 in connection with a large building planned for the maritimes. The article says:
Canada's first major monument to the fathers of confederation will be a cluster of classically simple structures with a crystal memorial hall as centrepiece.
Further on it states:
The architects estimate the cost of the building complex as $3.77 million.
Then, as we all know, Ottawa, through the National Capital Commission, is to get a fine new auditorium, and reference is made in a report I have here to the fact that it will be part of a centennial grant. Then, again, I notice a report in a Montreal paper that the expenditure of $17,500,000 has been planned in connection with an office building for Canadian National Railways. Again, in connection with centennial grants, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Dinsdale) said this in an address given at Halifax on October 17, 1961:
Spectacular new developments In our national historic sites and parks are under way. The much improved Halifax Citadel... is still highest on the visit list. In Cape Breton, restoration of Fortress Louisbourg will make this famous site of "battles long ago'' as widely renowned and visited as befits its pivotal position in North American history. Plans are already afoot to animate Louisbourg as a living museum. Think of the appeal this will have to the touring public.
We have not too many sites of that kind in the west. We have not too many battlefields to commemorate. We have been known as a peaceful race, perhaps until recent times, with regard to provincial-federal affairs. We do not criticize the restoration of the sites in the maritimes, or in the east, but we do ask that consideration be given to the construction of a coliseum of the type to which I have referred in order that we may properly celebrate the centenary. May I also point out that if a grant of the kind to which I have referred were made, among its main beneficiaries would be Trans-Canada Air
550	HOUSE OF
Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum Lines, the C.N.R. and the hotel Vancouver, which is in great need of a convention-type coliseum.
There is one practical suggestion that I wish to make before I resume my seat, and it is one which is receiving attention from a prominent architect in Vancouver. It is that the badly needed C.B.C. offices should be placed on the main floor of the proposed building with the coliseum above and storage space beneath and to the rear of the building, the studios to be built above the convention area. The advantage of this plan would be that the C.B.C. could move into modem studios in an area conducive to its operations and close to the two civic theatres now in the neighbourhood. This plan would also give to the coliseum a good tenant, and the C.B.C. would further benefit by being able to use the convention and parking areas when those facilities were not otherwise occupied. Certainly there would be extensive storage facilities available at the rear of the building and below.
I am sorry that all of us in the west have not agreed as to the size the proposed structure in Vancouver should be. I do not feel it would be wise to build a new arena with a seating capacity of less than 14,000. It is noted that the new coliseum in Seattle is to have a capacity of 16,000, and other coliseums on the coast have a capacity in excess of 14,000. Some myopic authorities have suggested a seating capacity of between 8,000 and 10,000. I believe that would be too small. I do not believe that is the trend followed in the construction of similar new coliseums. I am sure hon. members will realize that it is now almost impossible to get a seat on a Saturday night in the stadia in Toronto or Montreal for any national hockey league game. That situation has obtained for approximately ten years.
I cannot believe that those empire builders of sport Mr. Erwin Swangard or Mr. Eric Whitehead both of Vancouver would advocate or plan a coliseum with a sitting capacity of under 14,000. Those two gentlemen and other sportsminded individuals like them have had occasion to visit the east and have experienced difficulty in obtaining seats at existing stadiums.
I trust that favourable consideration will be given to this resolution in order that Vancouver can reach its manifest destiny.

Yes, I think it is fair to say that the resolution will receive unanimous support from hon. members from the hinterlands as well. The construction of this building is of particular interest to the citizens of the lower mainland and hon. members representing those areas. We hope it will receive support from hon. members irrespective of their origin and will be given favourable consideration by the government.
I agree with the previous speaker that it was only a few years ago that the construction of a stadium, arena or coliseum would have been undertaken by private enterprise but the situation is changed today. Such structures are now looked upon as providing a public service. Their cost is prohibitive to municipal governments and private enterprise and so co-operation and assistance are required among private enterprise and all levels of government.
I do not wish to repeat what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) but I wish to add to what he said by indicating that I am convinced from my knowledge of the city and its growth that such a structure will prove of benefit not only to local residents but to Canada as a whole. It must be remembered that in addition to being the third largest city in Canada, Vancouver is the population centre of approximately three quarters of a million people. Almost one half of the population of British Columbia resides there. Under the circumstances our request for federal aid in the construction of the building will be understood. We trust it will be regarded as part of the planning for Canada's centennial.
It is well known how much we appreciated the assistance that was forthcoming at the time of the empire games. It is recognized how beneficial the permanent structures have proved to the economy of Vancouver and thus of Canada. Thousands of people from across the land attend games at the empire stadium.
As a result of the construction of this building we will be able to look forward to even greater achievements in Vancouver in the future. In my opinion the project is necessary and worth while. I am pleased that the planning is in the early stages and I trust the required assistance will be forthcoming so that we on the Pacific coast will be able to contribute to the celebration of Canada's birthday. The existence of the coliseum will provide recreation for those visiting Vancouver and will make a contribution to the economy of Canada.
If I were to say more I would be repeating what has already been said. I conclude by saying I hope the government and all

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, I express agreement with the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) to the effect that when something is for the good of British Columbia you will find all British Columbia members in favour of it. We are as one. This is also true of the proposed downtown coliseum.
We have a happy situation in British Columbia. The city of Vancouver is thought of as belonging to all the people of the province. Vancouver is a source of pride to all British Columbians. I am sure that all British Columbians and all hon. members of this house from that province support this resolution. This situation is different from that obtaining in Ontario, for instance, where one often hears unfriendly references made to Toronto, the leading city.
The private members hour provides an opportunity for hon. members to bring their views before the house. Although this resolution is of particular interest to British Columbia I shall attempt to indicate that the thought behind the resolution has an overall national implication.
I do not intend at this time to discuss the seating capacity or the details of the cost sharing arrangements in relation to the coliseum. What we require to determine is the principle that a project of this nature is something that cannot be undertaken solely by private enterprise or a municipal government. A coliseum represents a public service serving more than the locality involved and the cost is too prohibitive to make it a fair, reasonable or even a possible undertaking for a local government or private enterprise. There must be participation by all levels of government and by private industry as well.
Mayor Alsbury of Vancouver commissioned a leading Vancouver engineering firm to make a comprehensive survey and make recommendations with respect to the construction of a coliseum in downtown Vancouver. A citizens committee was also appointed by the mayor to study means of financing the project. The committee of the Vancouver board of trade set up to study the question last week released a preliminary report on the subject advocating a downtown coliseum with 8,000 permanent seats and provision for up to 4,000 temporary seats. Of course, the size will determine the cost but we are concerned with the principle of sharing of costs.
26207-1-36i
Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum
Throughout Vancouver there has been widespread interest in and support for a downtown coliseum. This interest has been persistent over a decade. As to the amount suggested, I should like to read from the report of the engineering firm commissioned by the city. They had gone into the matter in detail with regard to the present facilities provided by the city in the form of the Queen Elizabeth theatre. In this complex of buildings there is one room in which 2,800 people can be seated. There is a little theatre adjacent to it and there is a restaurant. As found at page 2 of their report they state as follows:
Needed also is a convention centre. Vancouver lias many attributes of a great convention city. It is scenic, has a pleasant climate and is strategically located with respect to all major transportation systems. Further it is well supplied with good hotel accommodation and restaurant facilities. However, to be successful in attracting conventions in significant numbers the city needs a centre to provide exhibition space, meeting room accommodation and banquet facilities of the type that cannot be provided in individual hotels.
Vancouver has already invested in land and the Queen Elizabeth theatre complex of buildings approximately $8 million. Further land acquisition and replacement of a fire hall will cost the city another $1,200,000. The feasibility report suggests that the remaining costs of building a coliseum should be shared equally between private industry, the province of British Columbia and the federal government. According to this report that would mean that the amount required from the federal government would be approximately $3 million.
The value of such a downtown coliseum to the city of Vanvouver is self-evident. The value of this coliseum to the province is also self-evident. But what of the national aspect? Why should the federal government contribute to a project such as this one? I have already pointed out that such a project is not feasible without federal participation. The motion of the hon. member is keyed into a grant because of our centenary. However, I should like to suggest that this grant would be good business in any year because of the foreign spending in Canada this convention centre will induce and the new business it will create.
Last year we spent $855,000 on the exhibitions branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce and $3| million on the trade commissioner service. These and other expenditures have helped to make 1961 a record trade year providing more jobs than ever before in Canada in supplying the goods for our export trade. We had a trade deficit of $576 million in commodities in 1956.
This year we shall have exported more than we bought and our trade will be at an alltime record level.

Request Grant for Vancouver Coliseum
But what of our balance of payment? I refer to the payments which we are obliged to make in the form of interest payments, dividend payments and remittances for various purposes to other countries. Not the least of the items in our adverse balance of payment picture is the balance with regard to international travel. This year I believe it is estimated that our over-all imbalance of all such payments will be about $1 billion. According to the travel bureau, with regard to travel expenditures for 1960 our imbalance with the United States was $87 million. In 1959 it was $97 million and in 1958 it was $104 million. Therefore in these three years our deficit with the United States with regard to travel was $288 million. When we consider travel expenditures in connection with all countries in the 12 months ended September 30, 1961, we find that we had an over-all deficit of over $185 million. For the years 1959 and 1960, our over-all deficit was the same, namely $207 million.
Now that we have solved our commodity trade problem I believe we must take steps to solve this equally major problem. We must understand that $5 spent in Canada by a tourist is as beneficial as $5 spent in France for $5 worth of Canadian wheat. That is why this proposal has a national aspect. That is why not only this proposal but other major developments such as the development of Garibaldi, developments in Alberta, developments in the maritimes, developments in northern Ontario-all developments which will bring in tourists not only from the United States but from all over the world-will make good business sense in building up this country and will help correct a situation for which I can see no other way of correction, unless by means of arbitrary government control in the way of remittances abroad. Some day this incubus we have on our back will come back to haunt us when and if the flow of foreign capital which helps us to balance these payments is reduced or dries up almost altogether. I therefore say that this is a good business proposal and that this convention centre, complex of buildings, or whatever you may call it, could well be a very large dollar earner for the dominion of Canada. I say that the revenue the government will get from the influx of visitors and from the increase in business could well be considered to be an adequate dividend on the amount of money they are being asked to put up; and after all, this amount is only one third of the cost.
In closing there is one other point which I should like to stress, namely that the city of Vancouver is the major Canadian city on the Canadian west coast. We face the Orient where our greatest potential increase in trade


lies. Japan is already our third largest customer. We face south to the fastest growing states in the American union. We also face south past those states to Mexico and South America. We are at the crossroads of world wide transportation systems. We are a logical spot in which to place this lure which will make Vancouver a truly great world convention city.

have listened, Mr. Speaker, with considerable interest to the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor), and I must admit that he has made a strong case for the erection of a coliseum in downtown Vancouver. In rising to speak in support of his proposal I should like to bring to the attention of the house certain other matters which might be of interest.
I agree with the hon. member's laudable objective but I think that the proposal should go further. Bearing in mind the hon. member's background and his great interest in sporting matters, we find that he has, of course, emphasized the need for a coliseum. I should like to approach from a slightly different point of view the aspect of international trade which the hon. member covered somewhat in his remarks. We in Vancouver are very proud of the fact that Vancouver is known as Canada's gateway to the Orient. I think it is very important that Vancouver should have something quite substantial and impressive to bear witness to Canada's growing maturity. I should like to see the suggestion put forward by my colleague expanded so that it would not only include a coliseum but would also provide for offices, shopping centres and facilities for trade exhibitions, all located in one central spot which might be called "International centre".
These are my reasons for making such a proposal. Both the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) have dealt with the need to increase trade. At the same time, more and more countries are sending representatives to Canada. We see more and more consulates being opened in Vancouver. From personal knowledge I know of one trade commissioner from a commonwealth country who spent two and a half months in Vancouver looking for suitable accommodation.
Those of us who have visited New York know how impressive Rockefeller centre is. That particular project not only is a great tourist attraction but also is a very busy and much needed business centre. At the present time Vancouver has some very valuable property situated downtown which is used for no other purpose than a parking lot. I can well

foresee that this property could be the location of an international square such as I have suggested and which would include the facilities envisaged by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.
I think it would be a wonderful thing to have a series of buildings erected on a square with a courtyard in the centre, and I do not think anyone would fail to be moved by the sight of the flags of all the different countries waving. In addition, if we had facilities for exhibitions from these various countries located around the perimeter this would not only be tremendously educational but would in my opinion add to the administrative efficiency of the various consulates. I have spoken to a number of architects in Vancouver about this suggestion and they are quite enthusiastic about the possibilities of such a project.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard brought up the point that he would like to see facilities for the C.B.C. located in this coliseum. The C.B.C. is located in my riding and because at the present time their facilities are somewhat scattered I did some research into the problem. The figures I have are quite interesting. I had intended to speak about this matter on another occasion but since my colleague has brought it up I think this is a good time to bring out these facts.
The C.B.C. has different locations for its television and radio studios. It has purchased property since 1953 and it now owns a property located on Georgia street which is 363 feet wide by 131 feet deep, the price it paid being $515,600. It is now eight years since the first purchase was made and a start has not yet been made on the erection of a suitable building. At the same time the C.B.C. has continued to rent premises and it has paid out in rentals and grants in lieu of taxes during the period April 1, 1953, to March 31, 1961, the sum of $591,028.09, an amount greater than was paid for the purchase of the property on Georgia street. If we add the two amounts together we get the sum of $1,106,628.09 paid out between 1953 and 1961. This is a very healthy amount and I suggest it could have gone a very long way toward a grant for the building of a coliseum or a project such as I have suggested.
I have put forward the idea of a plaza or international centre because we already have a large auditorium in Vancouver known as the Queen Elizabeth theatre. However, it does not fulfil the needs of trade exhibitions and, as I say, we have a property which could be used for the building of an international trade centre. My colleague has put forward a very strong case as to the need for a coliseum and, as I have said, he is interested in sporting activities. We join with him in his interest
but I think that if such a building were to be erected in downtown Vancouver it would detract from the purposes of a centennial project and, with great deference to my colleague, I believe that an international centre would be a lasting landmark and an equally worth-while contribution to Canada's centennial. I hope that other speakers will support this project because I think it is worth while. I will certainly lend my support to the proposals put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.

I should like to mention that the people I represent apparently are not quite so commercially-minded as some of the constituents represented by previous speakers who appear to be looking toward the promotion of trade and other commercial activities as a result of centennial grants. Our people would like the centennial to be celebrated by the promotion of those things that can be best undertaken by public authorities with the assistance of grants from this council, for the promotion of the welfare of the people through the development of cultural activities so that our hundredth anniversary will serve to improve our cultural opportunities.

Mr. Speaker, one might hesitate to enter a debate which would do credit to any board meeting of the Vancouver chamber of commerce. At the outset, sir, I want to congratulate the distinguished member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) who introduced the resolution. I have one or two reservations concerning the limitations of the resolution but certainly not as to the principle.
In introducing the resolution, the hon. member offered as justification for the expenditure, which I believe he suggested would be some $3 million, the possibility of holding a trade fair. This is an excellent idea. He suggested, also the possibility of hearing Mr. Belafonte. This would be somewhat dependent upon taste, but I suggest there are also advantages to this suggestion. The hon. member indicated also that the construction of this coliseum would permit us to save some money by locating the C.B.C. studios in the building. I have long advocated this suggestion any any means of saving money in the operation of the C.B.C. is commendable.
Nevertheless, I should like to express my reservation. There seems to be some uncertainty or perhaps difference as to the actual purpose of the proposed structure, and in addition, as to what else might be accomplished in the same area with the expenditure of the same funds. As anyone who has ever lived in British Columbia knows, one would hesitate to appose anything which might be proposed to improve this wonderful city. My reservation is, are we tying the hands of the centennial administration in advising them, through a resolution, always keeping in mind that the government must be influenced to some extent by the resolution were it to pass? I suggest that perhaps there is a strong inference this is the case. Nevertheless, the very fact that the resolution has been debated will, I think in all seriousness, be a very useful guide to that committee. A large number of members have expressed their views concerning the suggestion that we should construct a coliseum.
This is not a particularly new idea in so far as the commemoration of a major event is concerned. The province from which I come constructed two auditoria on the occasion of their fiftieth jubilee, one in Edmonton and the other in Calgary. These buildings have served a very useful purpose. The


moneys were derived basically from oil revenues. I can well recall the premier's introductory address to the legislature when he said that in commemorating the fiftieth anniversary of the province he wanted to be certain something tangible would be left so that the people could look back upon something more than just memories of bugles and drums, bunting and banners. I suggest that these hon. members from Vancouver have the same objective in mind.
I have here, in support of this argument, some of the introductory remarks made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in introducing the resolution to form the centennial committee. He made references to the necessity of developing something of lasting value in commemorating the hundredth anniversary of this country. I think, therefore, we can all subscribe to the principle introduced by the hon. member because he, too, wants to see something more than streamers and bunting for the people to look back to in the years ahead.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, my reservation still stands. Are we to ask the centennial committee to make this expenditure in the one area without anything more than a cursory examination to determine whether or not an expenditure of this type is warranted. As I said at the outset, the very fact that the resolution was introduced does indeed serve a very useful purpose. This is a guide to the way in which we hope, and I underline the word "hope", the committee will take up its work in developing a particular plan for Canada's centennial.
Now, sir, modesty will not prevent my mentioning that there are other areas that I hope the centennial committee will recognize. For example, we want to bring to this country an international event of some importance. I am speaking, of course, of the winter Olympic games which will shortly follow our centennial. I mention this just to illustrate the variety of subject material at which this committee must look in order to make a proper assessment of the best manner in which to commemorate this very important event. The winter Olympic games would be the most outstanding sporting attraction this country would ever see and therefore will require a great deal of money in order to put together the necessary facilities to make this magnificent area of the west a two-season operation rather than limited to the very few summer months.
I believe it is now six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

of the C.C.F. Mr. Woodsworth wrote a note to both of them saying, what are you going to do about old age pensions; will you bring this in if you have our support? They wanted his support. I also want to say this, without being facetious. A few months ago the leader of this government said that the issue in the next campaign is going to be private enterprise versus socialism. This session that same government has been making a pretty fair attempt to expand the welfare state in Canada, and we are certainly not complaining about that because the welfare state is the exact position in which we are. It is going to have to grow. It is an inevitable part of the transition to democratic socialism. I do not think many of us in the House of Commons, let alone in the general public, realize the extent to which under this system of so-called private enterprise we are actually in the welfare state. I was most interested, while making a compilation the other day, to note that the Canadian government is now spending over $3 billion a year out of the federal treasury on the welfare state. If you add together all that is required for pensions, for health services, for hospital grants, for educational grants, for subsidizing free enterprise, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National, the coal mines and the gold mines, you find that over $3 billion is the cost of the welfare state in Canada at the moment. I feel this is an indication of the need for speedy planning to ensure there is not a hodge-podge of legislation, of grants and of subsidies.
I mention this welfare state because of the resolution which is now before us and the $82 million we have just passed in the form of supplementary estimates. I was intrigued as to whether or not there was a recognition on the part of the Conservatives of the meaning of this welfare state and of the warnings that they have been given by the fanatical private enterprisers who do not think it is right. I was most interested in reading this remarkable publication that we receive every month called The Outlook, which is put out by a chap named Gladstone Murray. He is a responsible enterpriser and it is most interesting to note what he has to say on the front page. It is headed "A Warning Signal", and I can only assume that this is a private enterpriser who is warning the government.
All who are engaged in private enterprise are warned to exercise special vigilance in 1962. This is the year the socialists and their allies propose to take steps to prepare the way to gain control of this country.
I had thought that when the hon. member for Essex East was speaking he had this warning in mind. He might think that these

advances in welfare by the government tied them up with the socialists. It is interesting to note, after this warning on page 1, that we find what the warning is all about on page 3, where we read the following:
Under both the welfare state and communism the responsibility for the welfare, security, and prosperity of the people is presumed to rest with the central government. Coercion is as much the tool of the welfare state as it Is of communism.
I thought you might be interested in that in case you do, as I usually do, that is throw this paper in the waste basket before reading it. However, this is part of the attack by private enterprise and the welfare state and is also aimed at confusing advances and reforms with that dirty word, in many people's minds, communism. I do not take that attitude, and that is why I welcome any advance that is going to improve the welfare and the standards of the citizens of this country. Personally, I am not concerned with who was responsible in the past or who is to be commended or condemned. The past is past. Whether or not this is an election year, the business of government has to continue and adjustments that can be made in the economy in the interests of the people should be made. The decisions should be made on the basis of merit, not of political expediency.
We can do the majority of our battling, when it comes to differences in fundamental principles-there are certainly fundamental differences-on the hustings and away from the floor of this house. I think a good many of us realize that the proposal now before us is not the ultimate. I feel we have to recognize that in this great welfare state the requirements of the senior citizens can only be satisfactorily brought to a conclusion through definite planning to establish a basic minimum of security at decent levels. Then we can provide, as our group has pointed out over the years, a planned contributory system so that, over and above the basic requirements guaranteed as a right of all, there shall be the opportunity of achieving a higher standard through the contributions made during the period of useful work. That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Assistance Act to increase to sixty five dollars per month the maximum amount of assistance in respect of which payments may be made to the provinces under the provisions of that act, and to increase the total amount of allowable income, inclusive of assistance, by one hundred and eighty dollars a year in the case of an unmarried person and three hundred and sixty dollars a year in the case of a married person.
