speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE ASSISTANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
The amendments
proposed in this resolution are twofold, Mr. Chairman.
The first proposal is to share with the provinces, if they agree, a further increase in the maximum amount of old age assistance bringing this figure to $65 a month, the same as for old age security.
The second proposal, again subject to provincial agreement, is to increase the income ceilings covering both the assistance payable and the amount of outside income by $180 annually in the case of unmarried recipients and by $360 a year in the case of married persons.
The considerations which prompted an increase in the amount of old age security benefit from $55 to $65 a month apply with equal force to the maximum benefit payable under old age assistance. Certainly if it is desirable to raise the benefits under old age security to $65-and we all agree that it is desirable-we can hardly do less for old age assistance recipients in the 65 to 69 age group, all of whom are in need of assistance to a greater extent than are many of those receiving old age security.
As a by-product of these actions there are, of course, advantages in terms of administrative efficiency and of convenience to the recipients in having the maximum level of benefit payable under old age assistance the same as the amount of benefit payable under old age security when recipients of the former reach the age of 70.
Old Age Assistance Act
With the approval of the present amendments, Canada's provisions for old age assistance will compare favourably with any assistance program in the world. In fact, the new maximum ceiling will be higher than those prevailing in countries like Australia, New Zealand and Denmark which have a comparable type of assistance program. Furthermore, over and above our old age assistance maximum, there is the possibility of additional amounts being paid to meet special circumstances where the provinces wish to participate in this respect under the unemployment assistance program.
As compared with the United States, our situation is also favourable. In that country, for example, the average payment per recipient for old age assistance in August 1961 was $68.44. With the higher maximum of $65 now being proposed, it can be expected that the average payment under Canadian legislation will be very close to that available under the United States program. This, of course, is quite apart from the additional payments available in Canada under unemployment assistance for which, I might point out, there is no counterpart at the federal level in the United States.
On this matter of unemployment assistance, several of the provinces-and particularly those which have large numbers of people in high-cost metropolitan areas-have been making additional payments to pensioners over and above the existing $55 a month benefit. Based upon returns for June 1961 which are now complete for New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, the federal share of such assistance payments in these four provinces alone has been running at the rate of $8 million a year for recipients of old age security and the three categorical aid programs. Information of a comparable date from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfoundland which are also making additional assistance payments shared by the federal government is not yet available. It is apparent, however, that the total federal share in the current fiscal year will exceed $10 million.
The increase in maximum old age assistance benefits of $10 a month or $120 a year necessitates, of course, an adjustment in the overall income ceilings on the basis of which eligibility for assistance is determined. As the resolution indicates, the maximum allowable income, inclusive of benefits, for a single person is to be raised by $180 a year and for a married person by $360 a year.
The committee will no doubt have noted that these new levels go beyond what would be required to permit recipients to receive the full benefit of the increase in maximum payments. This has been accomplished through

Old Age Assistance Act an increase of 20 per cent in the amount of outside income a recipient may have without reduction of the maximum benefit. This means simply that a recipient can now earn more money before his pension benefit is affected.
The pattern of administration for old age assistance, of course, has been developed on the basis of co-operation with the provinces which for the purpose of this program include the territories. The federal treasury contributes 50 per cent of the cost of payments made by the provinces to the individual recipients. Under these arrangements, implementation of the higher maximum benefit and the higher income ceilings now being proposed will depend upon action being taken by each province. We sincerely hope that the provinces will consider it possible, as they have in the past, to make these new increases available to the recipients of old age assistance within their respective jurisdictions.
In March, 1961, there were 100,184 recipients under the old age assistance program. It is anticipated that the proposals now before the house will cost something in the order of $14.4 million of which the federal share will be $7.2 million. I think that is all I need say at this stage, Mr. Chairman, and I trust that the resolution will receive the unanimous support of the house.

Old Age Assistance Act
I do not say the minister should wait until that consent is obtained. Of course, this parliament is sovereign within those matters coming within section 91 of the British North America Act. It ought to be possible, when we are considering a measure such as this, not to mislead the Canadian people into believing that because we pass this particular measure and it becomes law, it will mean that there will be one additional cent in the pockets of those who are able to qualify for assistance under the Old Age Assistance Act. Until each province tells us that they accept this measure we will have had only a declaration of intention from this federal parliament. This is another device by this government, another fagade, in their pre-election attempt, to convey the impression that more is being done when such is not the case.
Now, we say that this amount is inadequate.
